title: API Ops Fieldplay — Rapid recovery notes for edge degradations
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is an operator-focused pocket runbook for rapid triage and recommended temporary mitigations when the Redwood API surface shows common edge degradations: high timeout rates, bursts of 429s, degraded streaming (SSE/HTTP chunking problems), and elevated general error rates. This is intended as a lightweight fieldplay reference for oncall responders to get services stable quickly while upstream engineers work a durable fix.

Quick incident classification (first 5 minutes):
- Timeout spike: client latencies exceed SLO, 5xx/timeout traces climb, slowest p50->p99 delta grows. Check proxies/gateways and model backend.
- 429 surge: rate-limit responses spike; confirm whether origin (edge) or downstream (model pool) is issuing 429s.
- Streaming degradation: clients receive truncated SSE/chunked payloads, frequent connection resets, or very slow chunk delivery.
- Elevated error rate: 5xx percentage increases across endpoints, or specific model endpoints show failures.

High-level triage checklist (order matters):
1) Confirm scope and blast radius
   - Slack/ops channel: create incident thread and set initial severity.
   - Determine customer-visible impact (some customers, all, specific regions).
   - Identify deploys/rollouts in last 30 min (check CI/CD links).
2) Surface telemetry (run these immediately):
   - Grafana panels: API error-rate, latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), requests/sec, 429 count, streaming disconnects.
   - Prometheus quick queries (examples):
     - api_request_errors_total{job="edge-proxy"} by (status)
     - rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]) to see p95 shift
     - sum(rate(api_responses_total{code="429"}[1m]))
   - Check serving runtime metrics: GPU utilization, queue depth, outstanding KV cache hit rate.
3) Correlate downstream capacity
   - Check model pool replicas, queue length, rejection rates.
   - If GPU pods are OOMing or restarting, mark as capacity failure.
4) Check network and infra signals
   - K8s node events, cloud LB health checks, VPC route changes.

Targeted quick mitigations (apply one at a time, observe):
A) Reduce ingress pressure (fast):
   - Enable conservative rate-limiting throttles at ingress (edge) to protect backend. Temporary policy: 10–20% of normal QPS to mitigate cascading failures.
   - If using API keys, set per-key throttles for heavy keys identified in request logs.
   - Use a temporary global soft-fail for certain non-critical routes (return 429 earlier) to preserve core endpoints.
B) Fast fallback to lower-cost / lower-latency model variant:
   - If model X is failing or slow, switch to a compatible smaller model variant with same interface (pin at router-level).
   - Command pattern: update routing policy in console or toggle feature-flag that routes to model-variant-fallback.
C) Shorten max_tokens and response_length limits globally for the incident window to reduce tail latency.
D) Pause background jobs that increase load (async retrains, ingest, large batch exports).
E) For streaming-specific issues:
   - Toggle streaming to chunked-polling fallback: provide interim polling endpoint for clients if streaming proxies are resetting.
   - If SSE proxies (eg envoy) are losing keepalive, increase proxy idle timeouts and disable HTTP/2 connection pooling temporarily.

Fast tests to run while mitigating (examples):
- Sanity curl to endpoint:
  curl -i -X POST "https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_KEY" -d '{"input":"ping"}' --max-time 10
- Direct model healthcheck to serving-node:
  curl -s http://<serving-pod-ip>:8080/health | jq
- Reproduce streaming: wget -q -O - "https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream?input=poll"

Operator quick commands (k8s, LB, cache):
- Scale serving pool up quickly (if autoscaler slow):
  kubectl -n serving scale deployment/model-pool --replicas=DESIRED
- Evict and warm cache (prefix/KV):
  kubectl exec -n serving <cache-pod> -- /bin/sh -c "redis-cli FLUSHDB"  # only if safe; prefer key prefix deletes
- Restart a misbehaving proxy/router pod:
  kubectl -n edge rollout restart deployment/edge-proxy

Decision matrix — when to take each action:
- If 429s originate at edge (edge metrics show high 429): throttle ingress, identify abusive keys, fix misconfigured client retry loops.
- If 429s originate from model pool (model rejection): fallback to smaller model, scale pool, reduce per-request token budget.
- If timeouts and queue depth high but GPU utilization low: likely IO/DB or sync bottleneck (check KV store, metadata DB); consider pausing non-essential writes.
- If streaming resets but overall latency OK: check envoy timeouts, proxy HTTP/2 config, and TCP-level resets; consider switching clients to short-polling.

Customer communication template (short):
- Initial: "We are investigating elevated error rates affecting API responses. Impact: intermittent timeouts and streaming interruptions for some requests. Mitigations are in progress; next update in 30 minutes."
- Follow-up: list mitigations applied (ingress throttles, fallback model, scale actions) and estimated ETA.

Post-incident immediate next steps (within 2 hours):
- Revert temporary mitigations progressively, verifying metrics at each step.
- Preserve logs/traces for full time window and tag incident ID.
- Capture top 5 traces causing p99 latency and annotate root cause hypotheses.

Root-cause investigation pointers (owners):
- For capacity-related failures: infra + serving-runtime. Look into queueing latency, kernel scheduling stalls, or device-level errors.
- For proxy-level streaming issues: edge and observability teams check Envoy configs, keepalives, and gpibuffer sizes.
- For sudden 429s: product + billing for misbehaving client tokens, or serving-runtime for rejection policies.

Longer-term mitigations to propose in write-up:
- Harden graceful degrade routes: define explicit lower-quality fallbacks for streaming and generation endpoints.
- Safer per-key throttles with smart quota enforcement to avoid single-key blast radius.
- Improve autoscaler responsiveness for model pools; consider predictive scaling for spike workloads.
- Add synthetic streaming monitors that detect chunk-delivery latency and connection resets every 30s.

Appendix: helpful telemetry queries and example traces
- PromQL: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) by (handler)
- PromQL streaming disconnects: increase(rate(stream_disconnects_total[1m]))
- Kibana: searches for "stream-reset" OR "client disconnect" within last 15m and service:edge-proxy
- Example log snippet to grep for heavy keys: cat request.log | jq -r '.api_key + " " + .request_time' | sort | tail -n 50

Notes to oncall: this doc is intentionally concise — prefer small, reversible actions first. Record every step in the incident ticket and capture timestamps for each mitigation. If anything below is unclear, ping the owner or listed collaborators in the incident channel.
